CHART OF THE DAY: While the surge in Saudi oil production in October attracted most of the attention, there was another big jump: Iraq. 

Baghdad boosted output to a 7-year high of ~4.6m b/d last month (just under the all-time high of ~4.8m b/d of Aug 2019) exporting crude via Strait of Hormuz, but also pipeline (via Turkey) and trucking (via Syria) to Mediterranean Sea. 

Iraqi oil production has not only  recovered well above pre-war levels, but the country has much bigger plans. 

Last month, I wrote an @Opinion column flagging how Iraq is attracting international oil companies and could emerge from the war stronger: 

"Yes, Iraq is a risky destination, even more so today with a war raging in the neighborhood. But for the first time in decades, the country offers Big Oil the kind of returns it aspires to."

#Commodities:
#CrudeOil: Brent rebounds to USD 96.6 after touching a low of USD 94.32 earlier today, supported by reports of Iranian drone attacks on a US base in Bahrain and tankers striking mines near the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, the IEA estimates that global oil supply will exceed demand by around 2 million barrels per day this quarter, driven by a strong recovery in output from Persian Gulf exporters. Increased crude oil supply, however, does little to ease tightness in distillate fuels and LNG, where prices remain elevated amid a slow recovery in Middle Eastern refining capacity, production and shipments.

Metals: #Gold extends its decline towards USD 3,840 after last week's technical breakdown saw prices close at a 13-month low. Persistent inflation continues to fuel expectations of further US rate hikes, while concerns over the AI sector weigh on broader risk sentiment. #Silver leads the sell-off, dropping 3% to USD 47.3 and lifting the gold-silver ratio to a one-year high above 81. Meanwhile, #copper has slumped to a four-month low of USD 6.11 per pound, driven by speculative long liquidation as an otherwise constructive supply/demand outlook is challenged by the technology-sector rout and broad-based weakness in China's October economic data.

The US CFTC’s Commitment of Traders (COT) reports, covering positioning across US futures markets through 10 November, will be released on Monday at 3:30 PM ET, delayed by last week’s federal holiday.

Meanwhile, ICE Futures Europe released its report on Friday, revealing a 26% slump in the speculative net long in Brent crude to a four-month low of 134k contracts, while the gasoil net long fell to 54k contracts, its lowest since June.

Copper slides to four-month low as AI concerns and Fed outlook weigh

Copper is heading for a fifth consecutive weekly decline, with futures in London and New York both falling to four-month lows amid growing turmoil in the artificial intelligence sector and mounting expectations of further US interest rate hikes. The crisis engulfing Nvidia, the influential chipmaker at the centre of the AI boom, has cast doubt on the scale and pace of future AI infrastructure investment. This has undermined one of copper's key bullish demand narratives, with investors increasingly questioning whether the massive spending planned for data centres, power grids and related infrastructure will materialise as expected.

Meanwhile, a stronger dollar and rising US Treasury yields, driven by persistent inflation and an increasingly hawkish Fed outlook, have added further pressure on industrial metals. COMEX high-grade copper futures briefly touched USD 6.1165 per pound, marking a nearly 12% reversal from September's record high. The decline has brought prices below the 200-day moving average, with a sustained break potentially opening the door to further losses towards USD 5.93, the 38.2% Fibonacci retracement of the broader rally shown in the chart. 

While the technical outlook has weakened, attracting long liquidation from funds, longer-term electrification and grid investment needs remain intact, suggesting the current selloff reflects a reassessment of near-term growth expectations rather than a fundamental reversal of copper's structural demand outlook.

Hot US inflation, rising yields and a stronger dollar are hitting commodities, with gold leading the decline.

Meanwhile, crude and fuel markets diverge, natural gas and grains rebound, and energy equities outperform miners.
